# Diagnosing a Stalled Power Seat on a 2000 Toyota Camry

When a power seat refuses to traverse its full range of motion, moving only about an inch before stalling, the immediate assumption is often mechanical binding or a broken motor. While those are valid possibilities, the specific symptom describedâa consistent one-inch travel in both directions followed by a hard stopâpoints toward a distinct failure mode involving the gear train or the motor's internal feedback loop.

The user has already performed the first line of defense: visual inspection. Confirming no visible obstructions, debris, or physical damage to the seat rails is crucial because mechanical interference is the most common cause of stalling in this architecture. If the rails are free and the motor receives power (indicated by the initial movement), we can logically rule out a completely dead switch and a seized gearmotor. The fact that the system responds with a 1-inch excursion suggests the control circuitry is functioning, but the mechanical execution fails to complete the stroke.

## The Gear Train Collapse

In legacy automotive seat assemblies like those found in the 2000 Toyota Camry, the motor typically drives a planetary gear set or a spur gear train connected to a lead screw or rack-and-pinion mechanism. Over time, plastic gears within this assembly can strip, or a retaining clip can fail.

When a specific gear tooth strips, the motor continues to spin, but the output shaft loses its connection to the seat track. This creates an "open loop" condition where the motor spins freely without moving the mass of the seat. However, because the failure occurs at the drive interface, the system often exhibits a characteristic behavior: it moves until the stripped gear disengages completely or hits the end of its free-spinning range, which manifests as that brief 1-inch movement before the controller detects a lack of load change and shuts down.

To verify this without disassembly, you must isolate the motor from the output shaft. If you can access the mounting bolts for the seat assembly (usually located underneath the carpet), disconnect the electrical connector to ensure no power is feeding the motor while you mechanically lock the seat in place. Then, attempt to manually rotate the motor shaft with a screwdriver or by hand.

If the motor shaft spins freely without resistance when the seat is locked, but engages resistance only when the seat track is free to move, and the movement stops abruptly at the same 1-inch mark regardless of manual input, the internal gears have almost certainly collapsed. The motor itself is likely fine; it is simply spinning an empty gearbox.

## Controller Logic and Feedback Loops

A secondary possibility involves the seat control module logic, which often uses a simple current-sensing or tachometer feedback loop to determine position limits. If the motor loses torque due to gear stripping, the current draw might drop below a threshold that the controller interprets as an obstruction or end-of-travel condition. The controller then cuts power to protect the motor from overheating on a no-load spin, resulting in the sudden stop after the initial inch of travel.

This behavior explains why the seat moves backward just as far; the stripping is likely asymmetric or has compromised the entire gear set's integrity. Reversing direction simply engages the same damaged train in the opposite rotation.

## Resolution and Trade-offs

Replacing the entire seat module is often the factory-recommended path, but it represents a significant trade-off regarding cost versus repairability. In many cases, the motor/gearbox assembly is sold as a single unit. If you opt for replacement, ensure the new unit is compatible with the specific trim level of your 2000 Camry, as mounting points and connector types can vary between base and luxury trims.

If you choose to attempt a repair, sourcing individual plastic gears for this specific application is often difficult. The labor involved in removing the seat from the floor pans, disconnecting the wiring harness, and reseating the carpet usually outweighs the cost of a new motor assembly. However, if the issue were truly mechanical binding (e.g., bent rails or stuck latches), replacing just the motor would be futile without addressing the underlying constraint.

Since the visual inspection ruled out external obstructions, the diagnosis leans heavily toward internal gear failure. The solution is component replacement rather than repair, as re-gearing an automotive seat motor is rarely a cost-effective endeavor for most DIY technicians. Before purchasing parts, double-check the part number on the original assembly to ensure compatibility with your specific vehicle identification number (VIN).
